title: Measuring and improving search quality with Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: Captures how users interact with search results using the User Behavior Insights schema, then turns those signals into relevance judgments in Search Relevance Workbench.
Lets teams test ranking changes offline before release; part 1 of a series.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion
authors: Aruna Govindaraju, Utkarsh Agarwal, Sean Bjurstrom

title: Integrate Amazon Redshift and IAM Identity Center with enhanced VPC routing
key_points: Redshift clusters and Serverless workgroups using enhanced VPC routing can now sign users in through IAM Identity Center, with token checks going over private VPC endpoints rather than the internet.
Lists the endpoints needed (Identity Center, plus optional Glue, Lake Formation and S3) and tests sign-in from Query Editor v2 and a SQL client, verified in CloudTrail.
Needs a recent cluster patch level.
services: Amazon Redshift, AWS IAM Identity Center, AWS PrivateLink, AWS Lake Formation
decision: Public auth path vs private VPC endpoints for Redshift single sign-on in network-isolated setups
authors: Maneesh Sharma, Jonathan Glaser, Nishtha Mehrotra, Laura Reith, Suchintya Dandapat

title: Deliver real-time data to streaming tables for Apache Iceberg with Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
key_points: Kinesis Data Streams can now deliver a stream straight into Iceberg tables on S3 Tables (or raw to a normal S3 bucket), with compaction done as it writes and tables registered in the Glue catalog.
Removes custom connectors, format conversion and small-file clean-up; data is queryable from Athena, Redshift or Spark within minutes, and an agent skill can walk through setup.
AWS reports up to 50% lower delivery cost than self-managed options and up to 30% lower query cost; AWS lists delivery at USD 14/TB to S3 Tables.
services: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Amazon Athena
decision: Kinesis streaming tables vs Firehose vs Flink/Spark for landing streams in Iceberg
attaches_to: aws-bytes: real-time streaming (later); feeds the Nov streaming-ingestion-path PoC
authors: Nikit Pednekar, Mazrim Mehrtens, Ren Liu

title: Build a real-time event pipeline with Spark Real-Time Mode on AWS Glue 6.0
key_points: One Glue 6.0 design serves three speeds from the same Kafka stream: Spark Real-Time Mode for sub-second alerts, a streaming job landing everything in an Iceberg v3 table, and a batch job for heavy Python maths.
Mixed-schema events go into a VARIANT column that is shredded into typed columns on write, so queries skip parsing JSON; amendments use deletion vectors instead of rewriting files.
Arrow-native Python UDFs remove the row-by-row serialisation cost in the batch layer.
services: AWS Glue, Apache Spark, Apache Iceberg, Amazon MSK
decision: Spark Real-Time Mode vs micro-batch streaming vs Flink for sub-second processing, and VARIANT vs JSON strings for mixed schemas
authors: Shoukat Ghouse, Danylo Prozorov, Kartik Panjabi, Shrey Malpani

title: Razor Group’s journey to a modern data lakehouse on AWS
key_points: Razor Group found its provisioned Redshift cluster was almost entirely ETL, so it moved transforms to Spark on Iceberg in S3 Tables and kept Redshift Serverless only for BI serving.

Five phases with old and new pipelines running side by side; most SQL models converted automatically, but a minority with nested JSON, QUALIFY-style windows and snapshot dependencies took most of the effort.
AWS reports P95 query time fell from 180 to 63 seconds and blended infrastructure cost dropped 63%; Iceberg time travel replaced costly full-table snapshot copies.
services: Amazon Redshift Serverless, Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, Apache Spark, Amazon Athena, AWS Lake Formation, Apache Airflow
decision: Keep ETL inside a provisioned warehouse vs offload it to Spark on Iceberg and keep the warehouse for serving
attaches_to: dbt-pipelines (Redshift Serverless as serving layer, Iceberg folder); aws-bytes: lakehouse (later)
authors: Razor Group — Yaswanth Kothainti, Shubham Purwar, Ravi Kompella

title: How Picnic configured multiple OAuth providers for Amazon MQ
key_points: Picnic made one Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ broker trust two identity providers: Keycloak for human operators and IAM for services on EKS.
Covers the broker settings and validation steps for running both side by side.
services: Amazon MQ, AWS IAM, Keycloak
authors: Picnic — Oscar Mapfumo Sibanda, Amit Singh, Ayush Kumar

title: Build with geospatial and variant types in Iceberg v3 on AWS Glue 6.0
key_points: Uses a fleet-telemetry example to show Iceberg v3 features in Glue 6.0: geometry types with spatial predicates, nanosecond timestamps, VARIANT columns with automatic shredding, and column defaults.
Replaces the usual workarounds of separate lat/long floats, lost sub-microsecond ordering, and JSON kept as strings or flattened into rigid columns.
Data written this way is readable by any engine that supports these v3 features; deployed with CloudFormation.
services: AWS Glue, Apache Iceberg, Apache Spark, AWS CloudFormation
decision: VARIANT column vs JSON string vs flattened typed columns for mixed-schema payloads in Iceberg
authors: Shoukat Ghouse, Kartik Panjabi, Shrey Malpani

title: Migrate an OAuth 2.0 authenticated Apache Kafka cluster to Amazon MSK with MSK Replicator
key_points: MSK Replicator can now pull from an external Kafka cluster that uses OAuth, so such clusters can be migrated with topics, configs and consumer offsets copied and cutover done gradually.
Explains the OAuth handshake, maps each supported grant type to an identity provider setup, and flags the network and TLS prerequisites most often missed.
Adds a proxy pattern for identity providers sitting behind an extra federation layer.
services: Amazon MSK, MSK Replicator, Apache Kafka
decision: Which OAuth grant type to use when replicating a secured self-managed Kafka cluster into MSK
authors: Subham Rakshit

title: Announcing in-place ZooKeeper-to-KRaft cluster upgrades for Amazon MSK
key_points: Kafka 4.0 drops ZooKeeper; MSK clusters on Kafka 3.9 in ZooKeeper mode can now switch to KRaft in place through the normal version upgrade, keeping data and serving traffic.
Older versions must first step up to 3.9; the post gives a pre-upgrade checklist, client compatibility notes and built-in rollback behaviour.
services: Amazon MSK, Apache Kafka
decision: In-place ZooKeeper-to-KRaft upgrade vs new KRaft cluster plus replication for MSK
authors: Austin Groeneveld, Ashley Millette

title: Amazon MSK Service 101: How many partitions does an Amazon MSK topic need?
key_points: Partitions set how many consumers can read in parallel, but each one adds broker memory, file handles, longer failover and replication load, so more is not free.
Advice: size from target throughput and consumer parallelism, stay within MSK's per-broker partition guidance, avoid heavy over-partitioning, and confirm with a load test.
Beginner-level explainer; there is no single right number.
services: Amazon MSK, Apache Kafka
decision: Few vs many partitions per topic, trading parallelism against broker overhead and cost
authors: Yashika Jain, Ali Alemi

title: AWS and DuckLabs: Building the future of analytics together
key_points: Amazon has agreed to acquire DuckLabs, the company behind DuckDB; the founders keep leading the project, which stays MIT-licensed under its independent foundation.
AWS plans to bring DuckDB into more of its analytics services; AWS reports DuckDB integrations already cut Amazon Quick's average query latency by 30%.
Short announcement with no technical detail, but a strong signal for single-node engines next to Spark and warehouses.
services: DuckDB, Amazon Quick
decision: Single-node DuckDB vs Spark/Athena/Redshift for small-to-mid analytics as AWS starts embedding DuckDB

authors: DuckLabs — Mai-Lan Tomsen Bukovec

title: PythonOperator and BashOperator Now Available on Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA) Serverless
key_points: MWAA Serverless can now run your own Python functions and shell scripts as tasks, where before it could only call AWS services and needed Lambda or ECS for custom code.
Code ships as a bundle in S3 and workflows are defined in YAML; the example converts CSV to JSON and checks the result with a shell step.
Lists limits to know before moving DAGs from provisioned MWAA.
services: Amazon MWAA Serverless, Apache Airflow, Amazon S3
decision: MWAA Serverless vs provisioned MWAA vs Step Functions for light Python pipeline tasks
authors: Pradeep Kumar Nalluri, Aritra Ghosh, Sriram Ramarathnam, Karthik Seshadri

title: GPU-accelerated Apache Spark with Amazon EMR and NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 on Amazon EC2 G7 instances runs up to 3.7x faster
key_points: Spark on EMR on EKS can run on G7 GPU instances with the NVIDIA cuDF plugin and no code changes.
AWS reports up to 3.7x faster TPC-DS runs than comparable CPU instances, and the post also lists workloads where CPU stays the better choice.
services: Amazon EMR on EKS, Amazon EC2 G7, NVIDIA RAPIDS cuDF
authors: McCall Peltier, Kshitija Dound, Kinshuk Pahare, Karthik Prabhakar

title: Enable cross-cloud analytics with Amazon S3 Tables and Google BigQuery, Part 2: access control with Lake Formation
key_points: Same BigQuery-to-S3 Tables setup, but Lake Formation holds the grants and hands BigQuery short-lived, scoped credentials for the data files.
Suits cases where several engines need different access to the same tables and grants should be managed centrally rather than in IAM policies.
services: AWS Lake Formation, Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Google BigQuery
decision: IAM-only vs Lake Formation credential vending for granting an outside engine access to S3 Tables
authors: Lakshmi Nair, Srividya Parthasarathy

title: Enable cross-cloud analytics with Amazon S3 Tables and Google BigQuery, Part 1: IAM-based access control
key_points: Lets BigQuery query Iceberg tables in S3 Tables in place, through the Glue Iceberg REST catalog, with no copy kept in Google Cloud.
This part uses plain IAM: an OIDC provider for the Google service identity, a role it can assume, and one policy covering both metadata and data.
Notes on schema evolution, metadata freshness and the network path.
services: Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, AWS Glue Data Catalog, AWS IAM, Google BigQuery
decision: IAM-only vs Lake Formation credential vending for granting an outside engine access to S3 Tables
authors: Lakshmi Nair, Srividya Parthasarathy

title: Upgrade AWS Glue jobs to Glue 6.0 with AI-powered Spark upgrades
key_points: Moving PySpark jobs to Spark 4.1 can break on removed config keys, Python library versions and ANSI mode's stricter casting, which is on by default now.
The console's AI upgrade analysis runs the job, fixes issues over several rounds, checks output with data quality rules and leaves the final diff for review.
AWS reports up to 36% better price performance than Glue 5.1 on a TPC-DS benchmark.
services: AWS Glue, Apache Spark, AWS Glue Data Quality
decision: Manual Spark 3.5-to-4.1 job migration vs AI-assisted upgrade analysis with data quality validation
attaches_to: aws-bytes: Data Quality Check / File Layout Optimization Glue jobs (upgrade and measure)
authors: Prasad Nadig, Keerthi Chadalavada, Rishabh Nair, Shrey Malpani

title: Introducing AWS Glue 6.0 for faster and more cost-effective data integration
key_points: Glue 6.0 moves to Spark 4.1, Python 3.13 and Scala 2.13, and adds a wide set of Iceberg v3 features: VARIANT with shredding, deletion vectors, row lineage, nanosecond timestamps and geo types.
AWS reports the Glue usage rate drops by 30% on this version, before any runtime gains.
Also brings new ETL features and library upgrades; AWS points to a separate guide for upgrading existing jobs.
services: AWS Glue, Apache Spark, Apache Iceberg
decision: Stay on Glue 5.x vs upgrade to Glue 6.0 (Spark 4.1) for existing PySpark jobs
authors: Aarthi Srinivasan, Angel Conde Manjon, Danylo Prozorov, Bo Li, Mohit Saxena, Kartik Panjabi, Shrey Malpani, Peter Tsai

title: Track SageMaker Unified Studio project costs with custom tags and AWS CUR
key_points: Custom tags like cost centre are not passed to resources SageMaker Unified Studio creates on the fly, so project cost can't be grouped by them out of the box.
The fix: EventBridge plus Lambda keep a project-to-tags lookup in DynamoDB, a Glue job joins it onto CUR data, and Athena with Quick Sight reports cost by any tag.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, AWS Cost and Usage Report, AWS Glue, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon Athena, Amazon Quick Sight
decision: Native tag propagation vs enriching the CUR with a lookup table for platform cost attribution
authors: Nisha Gambhir, Dr. Anil Giri, Ram Vittal, Satish Sarapuri

title: Long-term system tables retention in Amazon Redshift with Amazon S3 Tables
key_points: Redshift can now deliver its system table data to Iceberg tables in S3 Tables automatically, with a retention you choose instead of the usual one week.
Opens up month-over-month query trends, before/after checks on config changes, capacity planning, audit trails and fleet-wide dashboards, readable from Redshift, Athena or Spark.
Works on RA3, RG and Serverless, and replaces home-built unload pipelines.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, Amazon Athena
decision: Managed system-table export to S3 Tables vs custom unload/ETL vs third-party monitoring for long-term Redshift telemetry

title: Secure SageMaker Unified Studio access with SAML and conditional policies
key_points: Registers SageMaker Unified Studio as a SAML app in Okta so sign-in can be limited by network, device compliance or MFA.
Step-by-step IdP, IAM role and domain setup.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, AWS IAM, Okta
authors: Manos Samatas, Amit Samal

title: Querying raw log data using SQL and PPL with the optimized engine in Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: OpenSearch's new log engine stores data as Parquet columns alongside an inverted index and runs SQL or PPL through a vectorised engine, so raw logs can be aggregated without reshaping.
Walks an incident investigation one query at a time.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Apache DataFusion
authors: Kaushik Krishnan, Jagadish Kumar, Luis Tiani

title: Powering agentic AI with real-time streaming data on AWS
key_points: Three patterns for feeding agents from streams: Flink-computed features driving live inference while also refreshing training data in Iceberg, streams that detect a condition and hand an agent a ready-made context package, and continuous sync of state into the agent's memory or context store.
Detection rules live in the stream and response logic in the agent, so either can change without redeploying the other.
Overview piece across MSK, Kinesis, Managed Flink, S3 Tables and AgentCore, with no build steps.
services: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, Amazon MSK, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon S3 Tables, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
decision: Per-event inference vs stream-triggered agents vs pre-synced agent context for real-time agentic workloads

title: Fresher insights, faster decisions: talabat’s near-real-time analytics across AWS and Google Cloud
key_points: talabat's events live in MSK on AWS while analysts work in BigQuery; instead of writing across clouds on the hot path, they keep one Iceberg copy in S3 Tables and let BigQuery read it through a federated Iceberg REST catalog.

Compared three read options (cross-cloud writes, BigQuery Omni, federated catalog) against no-copy, open format, governable trust and low operational surface; the write path is one EMR Serverless streaming job per topic with a dead-letter table for bad records.
Cross-cloud trust uses OIDC federation to an IAM role, and catalog metadata syncs on a short refresh cycle.
services: Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, Amazon MSK, Amazon EMR Serverless, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Google BigQuery
decision: Cross-cloud writes vs BigQuery Omni vs federated Iceberg REST catalog for one copy of data read from two clouds
authors: talabat — Harish Ramesh, Lakshmi Nair, Raghunandana Krishna Murthy Sanur

title: Amazon MSK simplifies configuring custom domain names
key_points: MSK Provisioned clusters can now advertise a customer-owned domain name set once in the cluster configuration, instead of overriding listeners broker by broker.
Keeps client endpoints stable through broker scaling, cluster migrations and DR failover; works for ZooKeeper and KRaft clusters.
services: Amazon MSK
authors: Ali Alemi, Subham Rakshit

title: OAuth 2.0, LDAP, and HTTP auth for Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ
key_points: How Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ can hand authentication to an OAuth 2.0 provider (token scopes become permissions), an LDAP directory such as Active Directory, or a custom HTTP service.
Part 2 of the authentication series, with configuration notes and caveats for each.
services: Amazon MQ
authors: Vinodh Kannan Sadayamuthu, Sarath Kumar Kallayil Sreedharan

title: NaranjaX manages multiple Amazon MSK Serverless clusters in different accounts from their IDP using AWS RAM and Route 53
key_points: NaranjaX spread MSK Serverless clusters across many accounts rather than one central account, sharing subnets from a networking account with AWS RAM.
Route 53 Resolver rules let clients in any account resolve each cluster's private DNS name; teams request clusters through an internal developer platform.

authors: NaranjaX — Federico Ostrit, Hernan Carlos Antolini

title: Mutual TLS and SSL certificate authentication for Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ
key_points: RabbitMQ 4 on Amazon MQ supports certificate-only login (username taken from the client certificate) and mutual TLS where both sides present certificates on top of a password.
Explains how the two differ and which compliance needs each fits; part 1 of the authentication series.
services: Amazon MQ
authors: Harshith Mithamar, Vinodh Kannan Sadayamuthu

title: IAM authentication with OAuth 2.0 for Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ
key_points: RabbitMQ clients on Amazon MQ can authenticate with their IAM identity via short-lived tokens instead of stored passwords.

services: Amazon MQ, AWS IAM
authors: Vinodh Kannan Sadayamuthu, Paras Jain

title: How Zepto powers sub-second search using OpenSearch Service OR2 instances
key_points: Zepto moved product search data nodes to OpenSearch Optimized instances after load tests confirmed segment replication and a longer refresh interval were acceptable.
AWS reports the same workload now runs on two-thirds of the nodes with over 100% higher indexing throughput and 30% lower cost.

key_points: Overview of the ways clients can sign in to Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ: local passwords, OAuth 2.0, IAM, LDAP, an HTTP auth backend and certificate-based options.

services: Amazon MQ

key_points: Records which agent influenced which in a multi-agent pipeline as a graph in OpenSearch, so a bad final decision can be traced back to the agent responsible.
Separates influence from responsibility and suggests guardrails to stop repeat losses.

authors: Jon Handler, Smita Singh

title: How Autodesk migrated 2.3 billion documents to Amazon OpenSearch Service using Migration Assistant and intelligent routing
key_points: Autodesk split one oversized index into four domains, placing projects by size and routing each query through a DynamoDB lookup to the right shards.
Used Migration Assistant for the copy and ran several PoC rounds to catch routing and quota issues before cutover.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon DynamoDB, Migration Assistant for Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Autodesk — Ambarish Rao, Chengsi Xie, Anirudh Gupta, Manoj Kale, Priyanshi Omer

title: How AppFolio transformed its data streaming architecture with Amazon MSK Express brokers
key_points: AppFolio moved its Kafka platform to MSK Express brokers to get rid of long partition rebalances and manual disk planning.

Short customer story with little build detail.

key_points: Explains how OpenSearch offloads vector index builds to GPU workers and converts the GPU-built graph into one normal CPU nodes can search.

key_points: An organization trail lands CloudTrail logs from many accounts in S3, and OpenSearch Ingestion indexes them into one domain for security search and alerts.

authors: Jagdish Komakula, Aditya Ambati

title: How a team at Epic Games tuned Amazon OpenSearch Service for Fortnite analytics
key_points: An Epic Games team running heavy writes plus batch aggregations on OpenSearch right-sized the cluster, reworked sharding and mappings, and upgraded engine and Graviton generation.
AWS reports p99 latency fell from 380 ms to 250 ms, throughput rose 16% and cost dropped 10%.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Epic Games — Jon Evans, Aswath Srinivasan, Gena Gizzi, Rajani Guptan

title: AI-powered cost optimization agent for Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
key_points: An open-source agent on Bedrock AgentCore reviews every Kinesis stream's CloudWatch usage on a schedule and says which capacity mode each should use, and whether the account qualifies for On-demand Advantage pricing.
Also flags under-sized streams at risk of throttling; deployed with a single CDK stack, reports stored for review.
AWS reports the right mode choice can cut streaming cost by over 60%.
services: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CDK
decision: Provisioned vs On-demand Standard vs On-demand Advantage capacity mode for Kinesis streams

key_points: Old Elasticsearch and OpenSearch versions get another year of paid patching, at a higher Extended Support rate.

authors: Kuldeep Yadav, Jon Handler, Arvind Mahesh

title: Scaling fine-grained access control for enterprise lakehouse using SageMaker Unified Studio and AWS Lake Formation
key_points: Table-by-table grants stop scaling once a lakehouse has thousands of Iceberg tables across domains; the answer here is classifying data with LF-Tags and granting to Identity Center groups by tag.
Mixes role-based and attribute-based rules, relies on tag inheritance from database to column, and carries the user's identity through to query time in SageMaker Unified Studio.
Deployed with CDK, with CloudTrail used to audit who accessed what.
services: AWS Lake Formation, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, AWS IAM Identity Center, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Apache Iceberg, AWS CDK
decision: Named-resource grants vs LF-Tag (attribute-based) policies for lakehouse access at scale

title: Event-driven pipeline orchestration with Amazon MWAA and Airflow 3.0
key_points: Airflow 3 on MWAA lets a DAG in one account trigger DAGs in another via asset events sent through SQS, instead of polling sensors or API calls.
Asset Watchers free the worker slots that sensors used to hold, and SQS keeps the signal if the consumer environment is down.
Covers cross-account IAM, triggerer health, VPC setup and when Step Functions fits better (approvals, complex branching).

decision: Polling sensors vs API triggers vs SQS-backed asset events for cross-account pipeline dependencies

title: Transforming search at Delivery Hero: A migration journey to OpenSearch Service with radial search
key_points: Delivery Hero moved its grocery semantic search from a self-built Lucene service to OpenSearch, combining vector and keyword retrieval.

services: Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Delivery Hero — Sayan Das, Hajer Bouafif

title: Upgrade Amazon Redshift DC2 clusters to the new Amazon Redshift RG
key_points: DC2 ties storage to node count; moving to Graviton-based RG brings managed storage plus features DC2 never had, such as data sharing, zero-ETL, streaming ingestion and a built-in engine for Iceberg and Parquet.
Gives DC2-to-RG node mapping and three upgrade routes (elastic resize as the default, classic resize, or snapshot restore with an identifier swap), with Redshift Test Drive for validating the target.
AWS reports RG delivers up to 2.4x better performance at 30% lower price than RA3.

decision: Stay on DC2 vs move to RA3 vs RG vs Redshift Serverless, and which resize method to use

title: Streamline Apache Kafka cluster operations and migrations with Agent Skills for Amazon MSK
key_points: Two agent skills package AWS's MSK know-how for coding assistants: one for day-to-day operations (latency diagnosis, sizing with cost breakdown), one for planning a move from self-managed Kafka to MSK.
The migration skill walks discovery of the source cluster, compatibility checks and target sizing for Express brokers, with an optional performance simulation before cutover.
The pitch is grounding the assistant in current service facts so it stops guessing.

decision: Self-managed Kafka vs MSK Standard vs MSK Express brokers, sized from actual cluster metrics

key_points: The Spark troubleshooting agent already used for Glue, EMR on EC2 and EMR Serverless now also reads failed EMR on EKS runs, pulling pod logs, event logs and exit codes together to name a root cause.
Usable from the EMR console or from an MCP client such as Claude Code or Kiro; code-level failures come with a suggested fix.
No extra charge beyond the Spark resources themselves.
services: Amazon EMR on EKS, Amazon EMR, Amazon Bedrock, MCP
decision: Manual log correlation vs AI troubleshooting agent for failed Spark jobs on Kubernetes
authors: Vara Bonthu, Andrew Kim, Maheedhar Reddy Chappidi, Jeremy Samuel, Siddharth Kumar, Layth Yassin, Kartik Panjabi, Shawn Huang, Weijing Cai

title: Amazon Redshift multi-Region disaster recovery
key_points: Starts from recovery objectives and data criticality, then lays out three cross-Region patterns for Redshift: active-passive via replicated snapshots, active-active with both Regions loaded in parallel, and a hybrid that tiers workloads by how critical they are.
Explains when the automatic snapshot schedule is enough and when manual snapshots are worth the extra handling, plus the cost each pattern adds.
Stresses that DR only counts if failover is rehearsed regularly, not set up once.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon MSK, AWS Resilience Hub
decision: Active-passive snapshot copy vs active-active dual loading vs tiered hybrid for Redshift cross-Region DR
